segments.title: Reading the opening movements at the River Plate
segments.summary: A broad battle map shows the ships' movements at first contact and centers HMS Exeter's place in the opening action.
segments.body: A broad track chart orients the opening of the Battle of the River Plate and gives particular attention to HMS Exeter. Admiral Graf Spee is initially heading toward the British force when the opponents sight one another at about 6 a.m. Their tracks then begin to curve around each other as the action develops. The chart is useful for following the relative movement before gunfire starts, though it is a general outline rather than an exact reconstruction of every ship's course.

evidence.note: The transcript introduces the action map, its emphasis on Exeter, and the forces sighting one another around 6 a.m.

segments.title: Graf Spee opens fire near maximum range
segments.summary: Graf Spee opens fire within minutes of first contact, and the choice to engage near maximum range is interpreted as an admission of weakness.
segments.body: The engagement develops quickly after contact, with Admiral Graf Spee opening fire at about 6:15. Only a short interval separates sighting the British force from the first German salvos. Firing at the longest available range is interpreted as an admission of weakness. HMS Exeter has barely advanced toward the British force's intended attack position when the shooting begins.

evidence.note: The transcript dates Graf Spee's opening fire to about 6:15 and characterizes the long-range choice as an admission of weakness.

segments.title: Exeter and Ajax reach the killing swing
segments.summary: By about 6:50, Exeter and Ajax have reached their intended attack geometry and are nearly straddling Graf Spee, though Exeter has already taken heavy damage as the German ship's main target.
segments.body: By about 6:50, the British cruisers have maneuvered into the position they wanted and their gunfire is nearly straddling Admiral Graf Spee. Graf Spee has already turned away, while HMS Exeter and HMS Ajax fire from the attack geometry described as the "killing swing." Exeter has paid heavily for the approach because the German ship concentrated on it as the principal target. The rough battle map shows why the position matters while remaining a general guide to the ships' routes.

evidence.note: The transcript says Exeter and Ajax are nearly straddling Graf Spee from their desired position while Exeter has already taken heavy damage as the main target.

segments.title: Langsdorff and Harwood fight for different victories
segments.summary: The tactical choices become clearer once Langsdorff's need to preserve a working commerce raider is set against Harwood's aim of destroying Graf Spee.
segments.body: Admiral Graf Spee enters a kind of fight unlike its earlier attacks on merchant shipping, because the opposing warships fire back and press the action. The German ship had expected its smaller opponents to be easier to defeat, but the British cruisers attack as if they must destroy Graf Spee. Hans Langsdorff can count survival, continued operation, and escape to raid more merchant ships as victory. Henry Harwood defines victory as Graf Spee's annihilation. Those different objectives shape the risks each commander is prepared to accept.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts Graf Spee's earlier easy actions with the British attack and explicitly distinguishes Langsdorff's survival goal from Harwood's annihilation goal.
